"The focus of activities of the 1st" and that's Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, "was on reconnaissance of the general Vitinica area pulling out the 2nd Infantry Battalion from the sector of Kravica to the sector of Konjevic Polje and its consolidation. Taking and controlling the territory of the general area of Konjevic Polje, Lijesanj, and Glodansko Brdo, intensive surveillance in order to gather information on the enemy and repel their an attacks." And then "In the course of the day, the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade completed all preparations for attack on the Bratunac, Potocari main axis, but the attack was postponed because of the arrival of General Morillon." And then there is a reference to the convoy which I believe you referred to a moment ago in paragraph 3, where we also see, "General Morillon returned to Srebrenica with his escort. He wanted to come to the funeral in Kravica on Monday and meet with General Mladic." And then at the end, "Decision, continue active combat activities towards Srebrenica in order to force, disperse, and destroy the enemy's armed formations in Srebrenica, the remaining forces are to retain their present positions in a decisive defence and prevent the enemy breaking through on any of the axes." And it's signed by commander Colonel Milenko Zivanovic. And do you recall earlier we saw documents signed by Milenko Zivanovic referring to liquidating the manpower in the enclave? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you also recall yesterday seeing a document concerning an ambush which you said was probably people of trying to get to Tuzla where a wounded nurse was captured by the Serbs and killed? Do you recall that, that document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When a nurse was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, how do you understand this part of the document at the end where it says, "Prevent the enemy breaking through on any of the axes"? Do you have any insight into what was planned by the Serbs for Muslims trying to escape from Srebrenica in this period?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They planned to kill all of us in the enclave without any eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've told us your centre for investigation of genocide in Srebrenica goes back to events even in early 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In this period, in March 20th 1993, or this approximate period, do you see any significant difference between the dangers of what occurred in July 1995, events with which we are all familiar, and the situation as it was developing then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no difference there. The scenario was the same. With the exception of the fact that the massacre was not committed in the March of 1993, but in July 1995. And I repeat, had they entered the enclave in 1993, the massacre would have been by far greater than in 1995, for the simple reason that in 1993 there were close to 80.000 people there while in 1995 there were some 40, 45.000 people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence? The interpreter didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters did not manage to hear what you said, the last part of your answer. Could you repeat it again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. The 1995 scenario and the 1993 scenario were the same. The Serbs had the same intention, that of entering the enclave and committing genocide. They had that intention as early as in 1993. However, thanks to the UN forces, the genocide was prevented. But was to happen two years later, on the 11th of July 1995, when the Serbs managed to enter Srebrenica and commit a massacre over, I believe, according to my estimates, some 8 to 10.000 people. Had they entered the enclave in March 1993, they would have massacred by far more people because there were close to 80.000 inhabitants at the time whereas in 1995 in the Srebrenica enclave there were some 40.000-odd people. The fact that this area was a confounded one, was a very narrow one, the civilians were surrounded from all sides, shows that it was much easier for them to commit genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could I have an exhibit number, please, for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this document which consists of two pages in B/C/S and three in English with ERN 04267599, to 600, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D885.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I want to skip forward a bit and ask if the witness could be shown D229.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this -- yes. I was just thinking, Your Honour, perhaps this should be in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. If you don't think there has been one instance where I have refused such a request. So let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I can say, finally, if we could look at the entry of the 21st of March 1993, on D573, "The entire free territory of Srebrenica and the town itself were shelled, infantry fighting in the Kragljivoda sector and the fall of Kragljivoda. Infantry fighting in the Poznanovici and Osmace area, ten civilians killed, 30 wounded. Morillon is in Tuzla and then going to Belgrade." Have you found and seen that entry?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this I'm focusing on this date the 21st of March 1993 because it's an important one. Can you confirm or not that this was a particularly dire day, the 21st of March?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A very dire day for the inhabitants of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we have a document of the same date from the Drina corps command, 04267603. Would you say -- well, I'll wait until you have the document. Would you go so far to say it was a question of life and death on that particular day or would you not go that far?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, it was a question of the survival of the Muslims in that area. We are talking about 80.000 inhabitants. It was a critical day for the survival of that population.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this document, Drina Corps Command 21 March 1993, we have a regular combat report to the Main Staff of the RS army. First, enemy in the zone of responsibility -- my apologies, it's actually paragraph 2, "combat readiness of our forces." "During the day forces of the VRLPBR, the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, were actively engaged along the Budak, Pecista, Potocari, Bljeceva, Pale, Radonjici, Zalik frontline and targeted Lupoglava with artillery fire." Now, are you familiar with Budak and Pecista?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are they or are they not in the Potocari area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right next to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that on the 21st of March 1993 there was actually an infantry attack in the Potocari area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Incidentally you've told us this was Naser Oric's area. Do you know whether his family was in fact living in Potocari on that date or at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His mother, his father, his brother, and many other family members were living there. He was born there and his entire family was living in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, I'll just ask for an exhibit number for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this document which consists of two pages in B/C/S and two pages in English, with ERN 04267063 to 604 is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D886.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then we have another document of the same date which is 04267605, Drina Corps Command, 21 March 1993, regular combat report to the Main Staff of the RS, Republika Srpska Army. And again just under combat readiness of our forces, paragraph 2, "During the day, forces of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade were actively engaged along the entire frontline on the Jezestica, Vresinje, Stolice, Bljeceva, Zagoni, Borici, Dzogazi, Caus, Obadi, Ljuljaska, Pirici, Gornji Sikiric [as read], Orascic line of contact." Now, do you see that there? The forces were engaged --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was the entire frontline, as it states here, being attacked on that day by the Serbs, on the 21st of March 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could I have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there document which also consists of two pages in B/C/S and two pages being the corresponding translation thereof into English is -- with ERN 04267605 to 606 is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D887.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'm now moving to a different area altogether so we are finished with D573 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacirovic, in 1992, 1993, did you ever hear mention of the idea of a subregion being formed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late 1992, there was discussion of the establishment of a subregion in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And do you know who, if anyone, was putting forward that idea?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the idea of one of the most influential politicians at the time, Hamed Salihovic. He wanted some kind of political organisation to function there. However, this never actually did manage to start functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You say the idea was some kind of political organisation. Was it a political or a military or some other type of idea?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an exclusively political organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know what if anything Hamed Salihovic did in order to try to bring his idea into realisation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He tried to unify that political body. He wanted something to be done, but this was not successful due to the circumstances in which the inhabitants of the area were living. There was no chance because of the wartime situation, the shelling, people being killed all over the place. So this was simply an idea. But it was a goal that was never actually realised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: During what period was Hamed Salihovic to your knowledge working on this idea?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in late 1992 and early 1993, and all the way up to the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. However, I repeat, he did not succeed in establishing the subregion. The political activities he envisioned did not begin because of the reason I have just stated, the encirclement and siege of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally on this subject, during the period that Hamed Salihovic was working on this idea, to your knowledge, was he doing any work involving a prison in Srebrenica at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm moving to a different area. I would ask if the witness could please be shown P458. This is what appears to be a diary. Now firstly, can I ask, do you know someone called Avdo Huseinovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I would ask if you could look at a couple of pages of this document. In fact, I'm going to start with the later page. It's page 7 in English and in B/C/S is 03593132. And it's concerning 6/12, 1992. And it should be a page which, in English anyway, the words appear, "Mustafa Sacirovic born 1 April 1953 in Hranca, residing in Srebrenica Robna Kuca number six." Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you in fact reside at any stage in the Robna Kuca, number 6?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't live at the address Robna Kuca number 6. I lived in the Rudarske Zgrade above the Bosna cinema. It's a little way away from Robna Kuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the Robna Kuca is, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Robna Kuca was a department store. That's what the words Robna Kuca mean. It was a general goods store.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. According to this, Mustafa Sacirovic filed a report against Mahmut Jugovic in relation to the theft of a number of items, one is 4 by 4 metres of fitted carpet. Did you ever file a report against someone for stealing some of your carpet?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It also says here "he has a card signed by Naser authorising him to bring in suspects." Did you ever have a card signed by Naser authorising you to bring in suspects?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Naser was not my superior. My superior was the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic. I was never under Naser's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you actually have a fitted carpet when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Where would I get a carpet? I was a refugee. I had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do the events here, a criminal reports filed for stealing a piece of carpet sound realistic in Srebrenica in December 1992 when you said people were starving and being killed by shells?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is unrealistic. I don't know what this is. This is the first time I've seen anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Actually while I'm on this diary, was there ever a curfew which was enforced in Srebrenica, that is an order which meant that people had to be indoors after a certain hour?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then just still on this document, if we go to page 35 in English and in B/C/S it's going to be the page ending in 3130, relating to the 5th of December 1992, we see the same name that we saw a moment ago, Mahmut Jugovic, and then it says "At around 1130 hours, on 5 December 1992, Mule" or Mjul, "who was under the influence asked for two litres of brandy for 100 DM until the morning, saying he would bring six kilogrammes of grain." Leaving the rest of it to one side, do you have a nickname, and if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? People did call me Mule but I wasn't the only Mule in Srebrenica. There were as many Mules as you like there. I don't know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you drink alcohol?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't drink alcohol, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you put on the ELMO, please, the next page where we have a continuation of this entry number 7 of the 5th of December 1992? Yes. You need to move it a little -- yes. That's -- that's perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, in fact I've finished with this document unless there is anything which Your Honours wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps he can confirm at this stage while we are at this, Mr. Jones, if he was ever interviewed by one or two policemen on this incident that appears on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And whether he was at any time during this period, ever taken to the military police headquarters, interviewed there, and subsequently released. I mean, I think we have a statement on him from this would give us a better idea on what to deal with, how to deal with this part of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour, I'll let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was never brought in by any police in Srebrenica, and this document is completely unfamiliar to me, but this is not about me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that explains everything especially since he said there were several other Mules in Srebrenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I certainly do have an application to make outside the presence of the witness, at some point regarding there specific area of the document because it seems as though there is a misinterpretation or there are two ways of reading the information listed here, that it's not this witness that was brought in but was the other individual. So, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to pursue that, then in that case because I thought I'd made it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirovic, on this entry with which we just looked at it refers, does it not, to Mahmut Jugovic at the top. Do you see that, 5 December 1992, Mahmut Jugovic. You see that named, Mahmut Jugovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you agree that that name, Mahmut Jugovic, which we see under 5 December 1992 in the same entry which talks about Mule is -- also appears under the 6th of December 1992 where we saw your name, Mustafa Sacirovic, and then we see again a reference to Mahmut Jugovic? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that Mahmut Jugovic, according to both entries, resided in Srebrenica, Robna Kuca number 8?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did or not. I don't know the man and I have no idea where he resided.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as submissions on this subject is concerned we can do it at some other stage, obviously without the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we are dealing with just a few more documents. The next one is 02075798. Sokolac collection. And it's addressed to the OS Armed Forces Operations Staff Srebrenica. It says "report submitted by Mustafa Sacirovic, Mule." I'll let you have a look at that. Now, I've given you an opportunity to look at that document. But this purports to be a report submitted by Mustafa Sacirovic, Mule, to the operations staff Srebrenica. Did you -- did you ever send reports to the operations staff Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only reports I made went to Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, the president of the War Presidency. I worked for no one else, nor did I submit reports to anyone else or any other group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And there is a signature here. Do you recognise that as being your signature or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature resembles my signature to some extent, but this is not a document I drew up and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at all the places which are named in this document. It's a report on a field inspection from the 27th of October to the 1st of November, and a large number of places are mentioned. I won't read them all because you can see them. But I'll just ask you this. Was it possible in October --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Was it possible in late October 1992, to visit all the places referred to in this document in three days, given the conditions at the time in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't believe it was possible because these were all peripheral areas exposed to shelling and attacks. I don't think anyone could have visited all these places in such a brief space of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At the end of this document we see the words in B/C/S [B/C/S spoken]. Do you see those two words?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is the word [B/C/S spoken] written in the Ekavian or in the Ijekavian dialect?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in the Ekavica dialect. There was written by someone who is illiterate and who is mixing up the two dialects. Ekavski and Ijekavski.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Who uses the Ekavian dialect, Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ekavian dialect is used mostly by Serbs. Muslims mostly speak the Ijekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd ask for an exhibit number for this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document which consists of two pages, one B/C/S, one in English, with ERN 02075798 is being tendered and received and marked as Defence Exhibit D888.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Next document is -- the ERN is 01838912, and it purports to be from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, department of the unified RBH veterans organisation, Bratunac union of veterans, Srebrenica, 13 July 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you see at the end, it's purportedly signed by Mustafa Sacirovic on behalf of that union. Now, is that your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like the previous signature, this signature resembles mine. However, I did not compile this document and this is the first time I've heard of this association, this organisation. It's something I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there in fact to your knowledge a veterans association formed during the war in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it. I tell you it's the first time I've heard of this veterans association. As far as I know, the veterans organised only after the end of the war. That's when these veterans organisations emerged, as they did everywhere in the world after wars. And this document is completely unfamiliar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was Naser Oric, who is referred to in this document as "our commander," was he ever a commander of forces from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This document also refers at one point to the following. It says: "It might be useful to mention that we liquidated more than 2.500 aggressor soldiers and put out of action even more." Now, did you ever hear when you were in Srebrenica the figure of 2.500 Serbian soldiers being killed, apart from by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's the first time I heard of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again we see here if you go to line 3 in the Bosnian, the word [B/C/S spoken]. I don't know if you see that, three lines down and it's the second word from the end, and then two lines down from there, deo, d-e-o, [B/C/S spoken], again are these words in the Ekavian dialect or in the Ijekavian dialect?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These words are in the Ekavian dialect and I see again that these two dialects, the Ekavian and Ijekavian, are being mixed up in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you accept the possibility that this document was written by Serbs using their Ekavian dialect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is speculative, Mr. Jones. I would skip it and move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We see towards the end of this document the words, "We do not want to be a minority among the Serbs or the Muslims." Do you see that? It's three lines from the bottom in Bosnian. Does that make any sense to you, that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't make any sense. I have no idea what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask for an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document which consists of one page in B/C/S with ERN 01838912 and the corresponding translation thereof into English on two pages, together they are being entered into the records of the case marked as Defence Exhibit D889. Of course, the English one will become D889(E).

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, we just have a few more documents. Now, the next document is dated 7 November 1996 from the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior, public security centre, Zvornik, and it's addressed to the district public Prosecutor Zvornik, "subject: Mustafa Sacirovic, supplement to criminal reports," and we go down to the bottom and it says, "Mustafa Sacirovic, a.k.a. Mule, son of Vahid and Fata," and then has personal details. And then, "After the liberation of Srebrenica in July 1995, the crime investigators of the Srebrenica SJB found written evidence at the Domavija hotel in Srebrenica which show that Sacirovic participated in the operations in the village of Zagoni, Magasici, and Kravica, where civilians were killed and buildings and other installations torched. Specifically as they were leaving Srebrenica the Muslim authorities left behind, forgot, some documents at the aforementioned hotel including among other things several certificates," et cetera. Now, did you in fact participate in operations in the villages of Zagoni, Magasici, and Kravica in 1992 and early 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Absolutely not. I worked for the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality and I did not belong to a single armed group in the territory of Srebrenica municipality. This -- let's call it a criminal report. I see it for the first time and I suppose that the Serbs having found all the documents that I worked on in Srebrenica, are attempting to demean the work that I carried out in my search for the truth and to discredit all the documentation that I worked on as an investigator of the war crimes in the area. This is absolutely untrue. I categorically state that I did not belong to a single armed formation or rather armed group, not a single action. I never went out to combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, you answered my next question as to why these reports might have been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number for this document and then we have three documents which can be one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. There document, which consists of one page in B/C/S, with ERN -- I'm not -- it doesn't have an ERN.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the corresponding translation thereof into English is being entered into the records as marked as Defence Exhibit D890. For the record, this document carries reference number of 13/02-230 and the date of 7th November 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes and we have these three more documents. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just so it's clear, Mr. Sacirovic, I'm simply asking for your comments on these documents. I don't suggest for a minute that there is anything in them. I hope that's clear. Now, the first document is the number is RR146576. And it's dated the 15th of May 1993. And we can take this quite briefly. According to this, Smajo Mandzic is providing a certificate that you participated in the operation against Zagoni on 5th July 1993. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ask for a certificate of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would I? I have no need for that. I never asked for any such certificate and, I repeat, I did not belong to a single armed group in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I can show you the next document which is RR146576. And this is dated 15th of May 1993. And again it's Smajo Mandzic confirming that Mustafa Sacirovic took part in operations against Magasici. Again did you participate in such an operation and did you ask for such a certificate?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, this is an illustration of the attempts by the Serb to discredit me as a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the next document which is RR146578 appears to be from the 15th of May 1993. Again, firstly, do you agree that apparently on the same day, Smajo Mandzic and Ejub Golic are issuing certificates in relation to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have no idea as to who was issuing these certificates, when and where, nor did I need any such certificates. I reiterate that I did not belong to any armed group in Srebrenica. I wonder what this is about. I wonder that no charges were brought against me for some alleged crimes that I committed in Srebrenica. You can verify my statement with all the survivors that I never participated in any such activities. And you can really investigate into this because this is an attack against me as a person and the work that I did. I am proud of what I did. These are pure fabrications.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very clear and that's very helpful. In fact, it even says here that you were slightly wound in Kravica. Were you ever wounded during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if these last two documents were authentic, both Ejub Golic and Smajo Mandzic would have been busy signing certificates for you on the same day, would they not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose you don't need to put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And exhibit number, please, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. These documents, separately marked as RR146576, RR146577, RR146578, each consisting of just one page and each accompanied with a corresponding translation thereof into English is being -- are being tendered as one document and marked as Defence Exhibit D891.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are on to the last two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The next exhibit is also RR146585. And this is allegedly from the armed forces of Vlasenica, Cerska command. This is one day later, 16 May, 1993. Certificate allegedly signed by Semso Salihovic confirming that combatant Mustafa Sacirovic participated in mopping up the terrain at those places on the 8th of February 1993. Again, is this -- is this true? Is this a certificate you asked for? Or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked for it, nor is it true. At the time, I was in the war hospital in Srebrenica collecting information from the wounded. I really cannot account for this at all. I reiterate that I did not belong to any armed group in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: According to this, according to the documents we've seen you would have been under Commander Smajo Mandzic, under Commander Ejub Golic, under Commander Semso Salihovic, under Cerska command, under Glogova Battalion, and elsewhere. That would have to be true, wouldn't it, if these documents were authentic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just briefly before the witness answers the question, I think counsel is reading into the document further than he needs it to. It's just that it's signed by a particular person, not necessarily that if Mr. Sacirovic had asked for the certificate that he would be under them, and I just think it's a stretch to now say that he would be under each person that purportedly signed a certificate for them. I think the witness has already testified that he never asked for the certificate. I don't think the question is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may be right up to a certain point, Ms. Richardson. On the other hand it does appear from the face of these four documents that they are signed incidently by three separate commanders. So at the end, why would a commander sign this document and not some officer in some office, say, such as the records office or whatever? I think -- I think that's -- I do understand your objection, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can actually skip the question, Mr. Jones, because basically it becomes a matter of argumentation later on as to what this means and ultimately it's a question of credibility or probative value that we need to attach or not to attach to these four documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely, thank you, Your Honour. I don't know if the last one has an exhibit number yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it hasn't as yet. But before you do, is -- I would like to ask the witness whether he is familiar with the signatures of any of the following, Semso Salihovic, Smajo Mandzic, and Ejub Golic? Have you ever seen the signatures of these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am not familiar with their signatures. I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. This document which consists of two pages, one B/C/S, with ERN number RR146585 and the next being the corresponding translation into English thereof is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D892.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, finally, Mr. Sacirovic, how long did you continue to work in Srebrenica collecting information about war crimes and about victims of war crimes, doing the work for your commission? For what period?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked for the entire duration of my stay in Srebrenica except for 1994 where I was secretary of the War Presidency of Bratunac Municipality, although even during that period I worked on and off, and then this was the period of 12 months when I was a secretary. Then I continued working for the commission until the year 2000 when I moved to the United States. After the fall of Srebrenica, I joined the commission for the gathering of facts about war crimes in Sarajevo. That was where I continued with my work, and even today I am working on matters relating to war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And actually I think you've told us already but you were submitting reports to the War Presidency during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I think you've also told us that you have reason to believe that some of those reports were actually left in Srebrenica when Srebrenica fell and possibly discovered by the Serbs. Is that correct, you have that suspicion?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. There can be seen from their documents because all the collected documentation, video footages, and all the other documents related to war crimes including my reports which I had been submitting to the president of the War Presidency, Hajrudin Avdic, were probably found.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And, finally, I think you've also told us at the outset that you delivered material to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal concerning Glogova, ethnic cleansing of Muslims and the situation in Srebrenica going back to July 2000.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And before I present the last exhibit on that subject, just a correction to the transcript. I believe you said that the documents -- you stated your reports were probably found by the Serbs, is that correct? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You explain that as the possible motive for why documents might have been forged, to implicate you in crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the main reason why my work should be discredited, belittled, and in order to detract from the value of the documents that I discovered on -- in my search for the truth. But none of the matters contained in my reports were exaggerated. I was only dealing with facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And the last exhibit has an ERN number 01025178. If that could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it has your name at the top, and then the Tribunal. "Minutes on handover of documentation related to war crimes committed in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war in 1992 to 1995. On 29 July 2000 in the premises of CSB Tuzla, handover of the documentation was carried out between Mustafa Sacirovic and Mr. Valerio Geps Aquila, investigator from The Hague. Mustafa Sacirovic handed over the following documentation," and then there is a list and then there are signatures at the end for yourself and for the Tribunal. Is that correct? Is that your signature firstly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you indeed hand over all the material cited here to the Prosecution more than five years ago, in July 2000?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this document which consists of one pages in B/C/S -- one page in B/C/S and two in English and with ERN 01025178 is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D893.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Jones. Mr. Sacirovic, Mr. Jones has finished with his examination-in-chief, which means we will now start with the cross-examination. Your responsibility pursuant to your solemn declaration that you made yesterday is to answer the questions that Ms. Richardson will be putting to you in the same honest manner and truthful manner in which you have answered the questions put to you by the Defence. In other words, you have no right to draw a distinction between when you're being asked questions by the Defence and when you are being asked questions by the Prosecution simply because you happen to be a Defence witness. Your responsibility is to answer all questions truthfully and to the best of your ability and knowledge. Now, Ms. Richardson, would you like to start now or do you prefer to have the break now and start and continue after the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's perhaps best to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought would you prefer that actually that's why I ask you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break starting from now and continue after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson. [Microphone not activated] One hour less five minutes and then you will earn the gratitude of the Trial Chamber if you manage to finish your cross-examination by the end of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll keep that in mind, Your Honour, and I will do -- try my utmost to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sacirovic. My name is Joanne Richardson and as Your Honour indicated I am a member of the Prosecution team, and I will have a series of questions for you. And the purpose of my questions are to elicit from you information -- some more information about what you've already given upon questioning by Mr. Jones. And if I ask anything that you do not understand, please say so and I will rephrase it. If I mispronounce a name which I invariably never fail to do, please indicate that you don't understand which name or the village or the individual that I am seeking information about and I can gladly rephrase it as best I can. First off, I would like to ask you about your background. I know you indicated for us that you had started your investigative work with respect to collecting information on war crimes involving Muslims and we'll get to that in a moment. But I'd ask -- I'd like to ask you if, prior to the war, if you served your mandatory JNA service.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Would you tell us when you -- you served your service, and what your area of specialty or what training did you receive during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I served in 1973 at Pijonez [phoen] in the Tito's Guard. I was a member of the Tito's Guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what kind of training did you receive during that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You stand in solemn review. Whenever there were high foreign delegations arriving to Brioni we would be standing there greeting these delegations arriving.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it that you were also trained in use of weapons, basic artillery training?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an obligation of every soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. So could you tell us what type of weapons you were trained on using?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Use of side arms, therefore pistols and rifles. That's the only thing I know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you ever in the reserve police at any point prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it you were never a police officer either.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to talk to you about the reports that you compiled during 1992 to 1993. First off, I'd like you to explain the procedure itself of your compiling the information, and let's begin with 1992. Specifically in May when it was, I believe, you testified that the conflict broke out, you were living in Hranca and there were a number of killings of Muslims, and you began documenting, writing down, the information. Did you save the information that you collected at that point?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you made a mistake. I did not live in Hranca. I lived in Glogova. Secondly, I gathered information from survivors, eyewitnesses, and I started writing about the 3rd of May, the events in Hranca. Those were the first war crimes committed in the municipality of Bratunac. That was the 3rd of May 1992, and then on the 9th of May, in Glogova, that was when I started writing. I was born in Hranca. However, my mother had a house in Glogova and we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Now, with respect to the information you collected on the Glogova attack in May, was this information that you yourself had observed or did you later on talk to people and proceeded that way to compile the reports?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the information I, first of all, myself experienced and then on the basis of the information that I collected from other eyewitnesses, survivors of these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to the Glogova attack, how many witnesses did you speak to to compile those reports?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to many of them. I will mention one or perhaps two of them who were important. Two persons who survived mass execution in Glogova, Djafaticovo Kuthaus [phoen], Ibrahim Dervisevic, and Mustafa Golic, who was detained in the Vuk Karadzic primary school but managed somehow to escape the Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was it that you spoke to them? Was it in the month of May or later on?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Mustafa in May in Bljeceva, whereas with Ibrahim I spoke several days later after he managed to escape the firing squad near to a river there. They were lined up, but he fell into the river and managed to survive by feigning death. Having heard about Ibrahim's miraculous survival I collected this information. This documentation that I submitted remained behind in Srebrenica and that was why in 1998 or in 1999 I again interviewed Ibrahim and I took an audio statement from him after the fall of Srebrenica, both from Mr. Ibrahim Dervisevic and Mr. Golic. This was because all the documentation stayed behind in the municipal building in Srebrenica. In order for me to substantiate my reports, I had to interview these survivors again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And, now, you said you interviewed Mr. Golic in Bljeceva, and where was it that you interviewed Mr. Ibrahim Dervisevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also in Bljeceva, while they were still there in Srebrenica, whereas after the fall of Srebrenica, I spoke both to Ibrahim and Mustafa in Tuzla. All of these -- all this information is documented somewhere, the dates of the statement taking and so on. I managed to take their statements about their survival once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you took these statements, did you write them down? Was that how you proceeded to take it? Or was it done via audiotape? Maybe I should specify. The very first statements you took from these two individuals.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to record or -- and make either audio or video recordings of the first statements. I would write them down. Later on I used my dictaphone, normally used by a journalists, to record their statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. So that we are clear in the very beginning, in May, you wrote them down and then later on, when you took a second statement, it was then that you videotaped or you audiotaped the information you took from them? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only audio tapes. There were no videotapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when did you take the audiotapes, do you remember? And where were you? And when I say where were you, was this done in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said already in Tuzla. He already said that he did it in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are trying to confuse me. But I did indicate to you that I took their written statements in May 1992 in the general area of Srebrenica. I believe it was in Bljeceva. You seem to be provoking me, whereas I audiotaped those statements in the territory of the Tuzla canton which can be checked out in the documentation contained here in the Tribunal, and in my own documentation of the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richardson. One moment. Ms. Richardson is not provoking you in the least, Mr. Sacirovic. Ms. Richardson, here, has a very important responsibility that she must perform and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber will protect her as we go along if you become antagonistic to her. Now, you haven't answered the question as regards the date. When did you audio record the interview with these two persons in Tuzla? What year would that be? And if you can also tell us the month, maybe that would even be better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assure you that I cannot remember the month itself. My head is full of all these documents and information. I wish to apologise because it was not my intention to offend the Prosecutor. I may have misspoken because she put some of these additional questions to me. I interviewed Mr. Dervisevic and the other gentleman sometime in 1998 or 1999. I know that it was in the period after the fall of Srebrenica. There is evidence to that effect which could be produced at any time. Nothing was fabricated. After all, I did hand the documentation over to your investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirovic, with respect to other statements that you took and this time I'm specifically referring to statements that you took before the fall of Srebrenica. So we are talking about 1992 and perhaps 1993. First off, in 1992, once you went to Srebrenica, do you recall how many people you interviewed in, let's say, the month of June and July?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to several dozen of them, of victims who survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how was it that -- well, I'll rephrase the question. Did people come to you, just as a general matter in 1992 and 1993, to give their statements about what had happened in their particular village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I would go out into the field and take statements. Sometimes people would come to me or if I would hear of a certain person coming to Srebrenica I would go to see the person and take the statement. Whenever a need arose I would go out into the field or I would sort out documentation and hand it over to the president of the War Presidency. It was only in late 1992 and early 1993 that I spent all the time in the hospital with the wounded, and I would only go to the municipal building to obtain some information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In your taking the statements, let's first concentrate on when you were in Srebrenica itself, we are going to talk about the investigation into the statements you took in the field. In Srebrenica itself, could you tell us whether or not you took the statements down first in handwriting or were they typed up? Could you tell us the procedure? Was the witness shown the statement later on to confirm this is what he or she had said to you? If you could just elaborate on the procedure itself for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put these statements on paper in my own hand for the most part. We would use recycled paper, paper that had already been used because there was a shortage of paper. So we would use the other side of a sheet of a paper, and every single page of a statement would be signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were these statements, call them that, and perhaps you should correct me, were they actually statements or was it information that you after speaking to them compile and then gave it back to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, to make sure that you understand the question, what's being asked of you is the following: Which system did you adopt? Did you write down verbatim, word for word, what the person you are interviewing was telling you or did you make basic notes of your own based on what the interviewee would be telling you and then ask him to sign, or her to sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The person's statements were taken word for word. Person's name, place of origin, what happened, where, when, who was the victim, who the perpetrator. That was the order in which we took these matters. But we would put -- I would put questions to the person, the person would answer, and after the person signed every page of the statement, we would read the statement back to the person. However, the statement was handwritten. We did not have typewriters. When the statement was finished, I would take the statement and give it to the president of the War Presidency, Hajrudin Avdic, as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you also testified that you would cross-reference or check on the accuracy of the statement. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it. The information you received from various witnesses, did you check on the accuracy of the information they gave you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to illustrate it. If there was an event in a village where five persons were killed, and there were three survivors who were eye witnesses, I would at any rate take statements from all the three persons and take their statements separately, for each of the three, and hand them over as such. After all, I did not select the information myself. I did not look into the discrepancies in these statements. My job was to find the person, take its statement, and put down whatever the person saw. Even if you have two persons on the same spot, they will not see the same things. That's why I used several sources of information so that one, one day, when a person will be analysing these statements, a conclusion can be arrived at, whether the matters did happen that way or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it there wasn't always more than one person talking about an event. Would that be correct? In other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean, because that would confuse me as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed. I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You said you would speak to about three persons, for example, about a particular attack. My question is: Did there ever come a time when you spoke to one individual about an attack and not necessarily three or four or five individuals?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I was able to speak to several persons, I did. Where it was not possible, where there were -- when such circumstances where I did not have five persons, I only had one, then I would speak only to that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And if there was -- and if there was a discrepancy after speaking to that one person, you wouldn't necessarily know it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A discrepancy if he speaks to one? How would there be a discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase -- I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you only spoke to one person at times, if there was not several persons for you to speak with, and that one individual gave you information, I take it you would take the information being given by that sole person and then you would turn them over to the president of the War Presidency; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I would. Not only a statement belonging to that person, but of every single person, because I would take statements from every person in turn and then hand them over. Therefore, if I had one event about which I was taking statements from five people, then I would take a statement from each of the five persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to the information taken from these individuals, whether it's the one sole person or the five, you never looked into validating the accuracy of the information? In other words, I'll actually rephrase the question so that you have a better understanding of what I'm getting at. If one person gave you information, did you yourself look into the facts taken from that one person to verify it in any way?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Distinguished Prosecutor, I did not have a mandate of estimating matters or weighing them. If I ever learned of a crime having been committed there and of a person having been killed there, my job was to find out who the person was, whether the person was indeed on the scene of the crime, and if I managed to ascertain these things, then I proceeded to talk to survivors, if any, and then forward the information to the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was there ever a time that more than one individual giving you a statement, that their facts were different? When I say the facts, the circumstances they gave you in the statement vary from one to the other? Or did they all give you the exact same statement regarding an attack on a particular village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information was never exactly the same but they were about the same event. Every person provided information as they had seen things happening. For example, if there was a village with 30 houses and five people were killed in that village, maybe they were not all killed in a single spot. Maybe one person saw one or two people being killed. I would collect information from the viewpoint of the surviving witnesses, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what you are being asked for is what did you do, if ever, while you were doing this work, there were conflicting versions, not different versions, but conflicting versions of the same events given by two separate persons that you were interviewing? What would you do? Would you investigate further or would you just forward your -- the relative statements to your superior, to your boss, without comment and without further investigations? This is basically what Ms. Richardson is seeking from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in any case, I would verify several sources of information, but I would write down what each person had said. These informations were not contradictory. If there were witnesses speaking of the same village, what differed was the viewpoint of the survivor, what that particular survivor had actually seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, Ms. Richardson, he's telling you that he did not come across this eventuality or this possibility of having conflicting statements on the same events by different persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I suppose you either move to the next question or --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And indeed, with respect to the names you were given of the Serb perpetrators, did that information -- was there any conflicting information about the names given to you? In other words, did one person who saw perhaps the exact same event gives you a list of names and then someone else give you -- gave you another list of names either omitting someone or putting in someone? Did that ever occur?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It did occur. The difference was in that not every survivor recognised every perpetrator. For example, I don't know this group of people here and perhaps you don't know that other group. But in essence, an event would occur and the persons giving statements need not have known each and every perpetrator because the perpetrator would come from different places. So people would recognise those who came from places they were familiar with, and that's how they identified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that you had taken statements in the fields -- in the field. Could you tell us approximately how many statements you took in the field in 1992 and into 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where exactly were you when you took these statements? What areas were you in -- were you located in?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the free territory of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say the free territory, are you talking about the surrounding villages, including Cizmici, Bljeceva?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cizmici, Pale, Potocari, not to list them all, the villages around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you took the statements in the field, could you tell us how you went about doing this? Was It a similar procedure? In other words, did you take it via handwriting and then the witness signed it and it was given over to the president of the War Presidency once you returned to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. I would take it down in handwriting on an ordinary piece of paper. The witness would sign. If there were several pages, they would be attached to each other. And that would be handed over.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what information did you take from the individuals in the field? And by that, when I say individuals, did you talk to fighters or did you talk to civilians? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly with civilians that I spoke. For the most part they were refugees. I usually took witnesses [as interpreted] from refugees but also from the local population, where there had been shelling, killings and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And of course among these refugees there would often be fighters. Did you talk to the fighters at any point?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes. I did when I went out into the field to visit a village, I would also visit the men on the front line, purely to see where they came from and I even obtained information that there were refugees among them. For example in the village of Zaklopaca and some other villages around Vlasenica and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it you also spoke to them about what they were doing on the frontline? In other words, that they were protecting it from the Serbs? And you talked about from a military perspective what the fighters were seeking to accomplish?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you can consider this to be of a military perspective. I would ask them how they were doing, whether there was any shelling, whether the Serbs were shooting, whether anyone had been killed or wounded. Those were the usual questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned that -- you testified that you worked with Hamed Salilovic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a time, we worked together with Hamed Salihovic? No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I stand corrected. Hamed Alic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Hamed Alic was the chief of the communications and information service and I cooperated with him because initially he was our chief, in a way, until he left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where was Mr. Alic from?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know exactly where in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Borkovski [phoen], near Bratunac, where his wife was killed in 1992. She was executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you remember his wife's name?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halima, if I'm not wrong; I may be wrong. But I do know she was executed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like the witness to be shown Prosecution's Exhibit P90, and this is, of course, the book by Naser Oric entitled, "Srebrenica testifies and accuses" and it is in Sanction, Your Honour, the portion that I will be referring the witness to. It's the English page P48 and it's the B/C/S 02919305 to 9306.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: While the usher is trying to locate the page, before we go to that document, I'd like to ask you if you're familiar with the book that this statement an excerpt from?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You're not familiar with the book, "Srebrenica testifies"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The statement that you're looking at, and just for the record I should read: It's dated the 2nd of June 1992, "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, municipality of Srebrenica, commission for gathering of information on war crimes and depravities," and it is signed statement recorded by Mustafa Sacirovic and statement given by Muharem Salkic. Now, my first question is do you recall taking a statement from Mr. Salkic around June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the statement he gave was regards to the incidents or, should I say, what had happened in the Bratunac municipality around May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to take you to a particular portion of this statement. And it's the very last paragraph. It begins with the word "before the shooting," that phrase. Do you see that? Do you see the sentence "I fell over the bodies in the brook and, pretending to be dead, managed to stay alive"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you recall what Mr. Salkic told you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you recall some other information in this statement? And let me just read the portion I'd like to ask you a question about. It says, "Before the shooting the Chetniks took all our money, some 200 [indiscernible] billions and our gold and silver jewellery. The following persons lost their lives by this horrible crime, Miho Abdic from Borkovac [phoen] near Bratunac, Hamid Alic from Borakovat [phoen], Hamilija Alic [phoen] from Borkovac. And there are some other names. Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you recall him telling you that Mr. Hamed Alic had lost his life?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an error. It's not Hamed Alic. It's his father, Hamid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I noticed that, too, so I was about to react. The Prosecutor was saying the wrong name but the witness observed that himself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She didn't even say one single name right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll keep trying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, keep trying, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So this information leer is not about Mr. Hamed Alic, not the one you worked for in Srebrenica in the communication and information service?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this manner of examination is confusing for the witness. It certainly about Hamed Alic. The witness said it was about the death of Hamed Alic's father so what's the point of such a question unless it's to confuse the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this witness is a highly intelligent individual and can tell us if he's confused, as he's just corrected me, it is the father. I don't think it's necessary for Defence counsel to get up and state that the witness is confused when he's obviously indicated to us that he is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move and I think we can move to the same question because the situation, the picture, emerges quite clear from what he has already testified, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacirovic, and I hope I'm not mispronouncing your name at this moment as well as the others, but could you tell us whether or not you had any contact with Mr. Masic about the information you collected from the witnesses? And when I say "any contact," I mean during the period between 1992 and 1993, and thereafter. Did you -- did you talk to him about the statements you collected?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which Mr. Masic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. -- the author, the person who assisted with this book. Can I have a moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It is Najiz [phoen] Masic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you discuss with him the work that had been done in 1992, 1993, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was he aware, to your knowledge -- given that you hadn't discussed it with him, but do you think he would have been aware that you were doing this work, this very important work in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he knew or not. The role of Nijaz Masic in Srebrenica is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. While we have that -- while you have that statement before you, and this Prosecution's Exhibit 90, I would ask the usher's assistance in showing you some additional statements that are attached to this book, and please tell us whether you recall that you had taken these statements from these particular individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we may have to come back to this because we do need to give the witness the B/C/S and refer to the ERN number, and it may be a bit of a problem. Perhaps the usher could just leave it for a moment and I could move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the information you collected in the field --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A problem that's why I asked to you ask him exactly which Mr. Masic, because--

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- as you will recall yesterday we dealt with this during the examination-in-chief. These two persons, the witness and Nijaz Masic, seemed to be both authorised to conduct certain investigations, in the case of Masic into genocide, but the authorisation was signed by Hamed Alic and not by Hajrudin Avdic. So this is what emerged yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I was -- as a matter of fact had intended to ask the witness about that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically I don't know where you want to get obviously and I will not interfere, but what's the point of asking him whether he ever discussed it with Masic? Because he doesn't seem to give us the impression that he was pally with Masic at any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: He's already answered the question I was only seeking to put to the witness the whether or not the statements in attached to the book are taken by him and he's already stated that he did not speak to Mr. Masic about his work. So in the interests of time, I will get back to the portion of the book and it will be a very short series of questions and simply about whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- whether he gave the statements to Mr. Masic. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Masic? He would never have given them to Mr. Masic because Mr. Masic -- he was not answerable to Mr. Masic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed. I misspoke. Not given them to Mr. Masic but -- and he's already answered the question so I can move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, when you testified earlier you said that you took statements from individuals in the field. I take it the only person you gave these statements to, whether it was statements from civilians or fighters, was to the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Avdic? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And that last statement that was recorded by you, and this was given to you by Mr. Muharem Salkic, that document is dated June 2nd 1992. Do you recall at around that time, was it that you had been appointed president of the commission for gathering information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of June, you mean? Well, let me tell you something.
